I've been mulling over the implications.

  1. I don't think this technology is scaleable. It might simply be that a signal can only go back a few milliseconds in time. So, that narrows down what can be done with it practically. Sending stock trading secrets back a few milliseconds isn't going to give anyone an advantage.

  2. I don't think there is a practical way to harness the energy of electron spin to do work without breaking the entanglement (and thus breaking the machine before the energy ever gets transmitted). So, we probably can't "steal" the future's energy to power the electrical grid.

This may just be a curiosity which never becomes useful. But, here's an interesting scenario (which assumes point 1 is false).

A Bitcoin Miner wants to solve a hash. He has a time crystal and the technology is mature enough that he can transmit solutions to his time crystal in the past. So, a block is up for mining and he lets everyone else come up with a solution. Then he transmits that solution to the past and while everyone is working on the solution, he preemptively sends the solution to be verified by the network.

The way he gets away with this without tipping everyone else off is, he knows how much time it took for everyone else to solve the hash, so he submits maybe a couple of minutes before that happens. And he never submits from the same "mining" rig, so it creates an illusion that many people are "winning".

The biggest problem is, there is a statistical probability that a miner will eventually solve a hash. So, if a large mining operation is expected to solve a hash once a week, and 10 weeks in they haven't won anything, they'd get suspicious and the game would be up.

So, the "Time Crystal Bandit", wouldn't be able to submit every solution. Just enough so that it alters the statistics in a "statistically insignificant" way. Maybe he could get away with "cheat solving" less than 1% of the hashes.

Anyway, that's my rabbit hole. It doesn't create any "time paradoxes" as far as I can tell.
